howItWorks.intro: The calculator multiplies your selected per-class government fee by the number of classes you're filing in, then adds a flat attorney fee if you've chosen to use one. That's the full extent of what a cost calculator can responsibly estimate — it can't tell you whether your mark will clear examination, only what filing it will likely cost up front.

rules.name: Total Cost
rules.formula: Total = (Per Class Fee × Classes) + Attorney Fee
rules.explanation: The USPTO charges its base application fee per class, not per mark, so filing the same mark in two unrelated classes (say, Class 25 for apparel and Class 35 for retail services) doubles the government portion of your bill. The attorney fee, when selected, is added once as a flat amount rather than per class, since most firms quote filing assistance as a single package covering every class in one application.

howItWorks.outro: This is a cost estimate only, not legal advice. It doesn't account for office action responses, opposition proceedings, Statement of Use or extension fees for intent-to-use filings, or state-level trademark registration, all of which can add to the total. Trademark strategy — including the clearance search and which classes to file in — should involve a licensed trademark attorney, since a cost calculator has no way to judge whether your mark is even registrable.

faq.question: What does it cost to file a trademark with the USPTO?
faq.answer: The government filing fee alone runs $250 per class under TEAS Plus or $350 per class under TEAS Standard. A business filing in two classes under TEAS Plus pays $500 to the USPTO; add a $600–$1,500 flat attorney fee and a two-class application with legal help typically lands around $1,100–$2,000 before any office actions come into play.

faq.question: What's the difference between TEAS Plus and TEAS Standard?
faq.answer: TEAS Plus requires you to select your goods/services description straight from the USPTO's pre-approved Trademark ID Manual and costs $250 per class. TEAS Standard lets you write a custom description instead but costs $350 per class and typically asks for more detail up front. Most straightforward applications qualify for TEAS Plus.

faq.question: What's the difference between use-in-commerce and intent-to-use filings?
faq.answer: Use-in-commerce (Section 1(a)) means you're already selling under the mark and submit proof of use with your application. Intent-to-use (Section 1(b)) lets you file before launching, but after the USPTO issues a Notice of Allowance you must file a Statement of Use ($100/class) and pay $125/class for each six-month extension if you're not yet using the mark — up to five extensions, or roughly three years total.

faq.question: Do I need a trademark attorney to file?
faq.answer: No — individuals and most domestic entities can self-file directly through TEAS. But trademark law involves real judgment calls, like whether a mark is merely descriptive or confusingly similar to an existing registration, and a meaningful share of applications draw at least one office action. Many small businesses pay a flat attorney fee of roughly $600–$1,500 specifically to reduce that risk and to get the clearance search and class selection right before filing. This calculator gives a cost estimate, not legal advice.

faq.question: What happens if the USPTO issues an office action?
faq.answer: An office action is the examining attorney's written objection — common reasons include a likelihood-of-confusion refusal, a merely-descriptive refusal, or a rejected specimen of use. You typically have three months (extendable to six, for a fee) to respond. If an attorney handled the original filing, a substantive response often adds $300–$900 in additional fees; if you self-filed, factor that cost in before assuming your filing is finished once the application is submitted.

howWeCalculate.intro: Here's the arithmetic behind each result:
steps: We take your selected filing type — TEAS Plus at $250 per class or TEAS Standard at $350 per class — and multiply it by the number of classes you entered, giving the USPTO Filing Fee.
If you selected 'Use Attorney: Yes,' a flat attorney fee is added on top of the government fee to represent typical flat-fee filing assistance for a straightforward, single-mark application.
The USPTO Filing Fee and Attorney Fee are added together to produce the Total Cost shown in the results.
The breakdown is shown as separate line items so you can see how much of your total is a fixed government charge versus a legal fee you could negotiate, reduce, or skip.
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These figures reflect the USPTO's published per-class fee structure and typical flat-fee attorney pricing for a straightforward filing; they don't include office action response fees, Statement of Use or extension fees for intent-to-use applications, or the cost of a clearance search, monitoring, or international filing under the Madrid Protocol. Confirm current USPTO fees at uspto.gov before filing, and treat this tool as a cost estimate, not legal advice.

whenToUse.intro: This calculator fits the budgeting stage that comes before you open TEAS, the USPTO's e-filing system — once you already know, or have a reasonable guess at, your classes and filing basis.
scenarios: Before filing, to see how the government fee changes if you add a second or third class of goods or services to the same application.
When deciding between TEAS Plus and TEAS Standard, since the $100-per-class gap between them adds up fast once you're filing in multiple classes.
When reviewing an attorney's quote and wanting a baseline to judge whether the flat fee being proposed is in a reasonable range.
When budgeting for an intent-to-use filing, where the Statement of Use fee and possible extension fees come due later rather than at the initial filing.
When weighing the cost of filing in extra classes now against the cost of a separate, later application if your product line or services expand.

sections.title: What the USPTO Actually Charges
sections.body: Registering a trademark starts with a federal filing fee set per class of goods or services, not per mark. Under the USPTO's current fee structure, a TEAS Plus application — which requires you to pick your goods and services straight from the USPTO's pre-approved Trademark ID Manual — runs $250 per class. If your description doesn't match an approved entry, or you need custom wording, you file TEAS Standard instead at $350 per class. A software company covering both "downloadable software" and "software as a service" typically needs two classes (Class 9 and Class 42), so the government fee alone can range from $500 to $700 before anyone touches the legal side of the application.

sections.title: Use-in-Commerce vs. Intent-to-Use Changes the Timeline and the Bill
sections.body: Every application is filed under one of two legal bases. Section 1(a), use in commerce, means you're already selling under the mark and can submit proof — specimens and a first-use date — with your initial filing, and that's usually the end of the fee story unless an examiner issues an office action. Section 1(b), intent to use, lets you reserve a mark before you've launched, but once the USPTO issues a Notice of Allowance you owe a Statement of Use ($100 per class) to prove actual use. If you're not ready yet, each six-month Extension Request costs $125 per class, for up to five extensions — meaning an intent-to-use filer can spend close to three years and several hundred extra dollars per class just keeping the application alive before registration ever issues.

sections.title: DIY Filing, Attorney Fees, and the Real Cost of an Office Action
sections.body: Nothing legally requires an attorney to file a trademark application unless you're domiciled outside the U.S. — but trademark law has sharp edges: likelihood-of-confusion refusals, descriptiveness refusals, and specimen rejections are common, and a meaningful share of applications draw at least one office action. A flat-fee attorney filing typically runs $600 to $1,500 for a straightforward single-mark application in one or two classes, while responding to a substantive office action afterward often adds another $300 to $900 if the original filing wasn't done by counsel. Many small businesses treat the attorney fee as insurance against a refusal that would otherwise force a second filing fee down the road. Whatever you decide about representation, the clearance search and class selection are the two decisions worth paying a trademark attorney for even if you self-file the application itself — a weak clearance search is the single most common reason registrations get challenged or refused later.

howToSteps.title: Count Your Classes
howToSteps.description: Work out how many Nice Classification classes your goods or services fall under — for example, Class 25 for clothing and Class 35 for an online store selling it count as two separate classes.

howToSteps.title: Choose TEAS Plus or TEAS Standard
howToSteps.description: Select TEAS Plus ($250/class) if your goods/services description matches an entry in the USPTO's Trademark ID Manual exactly, or TEAS Standard ($350/class) if you need custom wording instead.

howToSteps.title: Decide Whether You'll Use an Attorney
howToSteps.description: Select 'Yes' to add a typical flat attorney fee for filing assistance, or 'No' to see the bare USPTO government fee on its own.

howToSteps.title: Click Calculate
howToSteps.description: The calculator multiplies your per-class fee by your number of classes and adds the attorney fee on top if you selected one.

howToSteps.title: Review the Breakdown
howToSteps.description: Check the USPTO Filing Fee, Attorney Fee, and Total Cost as separate line items so you can see how much is a fixed government charge versus a fee you could negotiate or skip.

tips: Match your classes to what you actually sell or plan to sell soon — filing in a class you're not yet using (under intent-to-use) commits you to a Statement of Use and possibly extension fees down the line.
TEAS Plus saves $100 per class versus TEAS Standard, but only works if your goods/services description matches an entry in the USPTO's Trademark ID Manual word-for-word.
Budget separately for a knockout or comprehensive clearance search before filing — a mark that sounds available can still infringe an existing registration in the same class.
If you're filing intent-to-use, plan ahead for the Statement of Use fee ($100/class) and possibly one or more $125-per-class extension requests before registration can issue.

Get an attorney's flat-fee quote in writing before filing, and ask explicitly whether office action responses are included or billed separately — that's where self-filers most often get caught off guard.
